text: PSR J0437−4715 is a pulsar discovered in the Parkes 70 cm survey and is recognized as the closest and brightest millisecond pulsar (MSP) known. It rotates at a rate of 173.68 times per second, completing one rotation every 5.7574 milliseconds, and emits a searchlight-like radio beam that sweeps past Earth with each rotation. Prior to the Gaia mission, it was the most precisely located object outside the Solar System, with a distance recorded in 2008 as 156.3±1.3 parsecs or 509.8±4.2 light-years. This pulsar is considered the most stable natural clock known and is debatably more stable than man-made atomic clocks, with a stability of about one part in 10¹⁵; two other pulsars, PSR B1855+09 and PSR B1937+21, exhibit stability comparable to atomic clocks at about three parts in 10¹⁴. PSR J0437−4715 is the first MSP to have its X-ray emission detected and studied in detail and is one of only two pulsars for which the full three-dimensional orientation of its orbit has been determined. Optical observations suggest that its binary companion is most likely a low-mass helium white dwarf, with the pulsar having a mass of about 1.4 solar masses (M☉) and the companion approximately 0.25 M☉. The two objects orbit each other every 5.741 days in nearly perfect circular orbits.
